comments.subject: Feedback: Disability Community Concerns, PSFSS meeting 10/17
comments.text:
Dear City Council Members Jimenez, Doan, Kamei, Torres, and Batra:
I am writing today regarding item (d)3 on the October 17 agenda for the Public Safety, Finance, and Strategic Support
Committee (PSFSS), Options for Expanding Alternative Response and Co-Response Programs to 911 Calls for Service.
Parents Helping Parents is the lead agency in Santa Clara County supporting parents of children with disabilities; each
year over 6,000 county residents are served by PHP.
We ask members of PSFSS to defer accepting the report and direct staff to return within 60 days with updated
recommendations for additional alternative response options to explore TRUST responses to the disability community
beyond mental health disabilities.
Our concern is around Finding #1 and FInding #3:
Finding #1: Finding #1 preference for alternative response The first finding, that members of disabled communities and
their representatives, prefer alternative response programs over co-response programs (with law enforcement), is the
key finding, and all decisions made by city officials should follow from it.
Finding #3: As the staff report details, “Many community members and advocates also supported prioritizing further
investment and resources in alternative response and community-based programs over co-response programs, as
alternative team response can create more equitable outcomes for communities of color and others
disproportionately impacted by the criminal justice system.” (emphasis added). We do agree with the recommendation
to hire more clinicians and others with the skills to communicate with people with particular disabilities, such as those
fluent in American Sign Language.
San José should strive to remove armed officers from as many situations as possible rather than put the onus of safety
on community members, as detailed in several examples from other jurisdictions cited in the staff report.
We would respectfully like to remind committee members that currently 1 in 36 children in our region and our country
are born with autism, and that 20% of the population has disabilities. People of color with disabilities are more at risk
than any other segment of the population when police become involved. In a recent town hall meeting at Parents
Helping Parents, we collected survey responses from families on the top eight public policy priorities for their families: a
full two-thirds of our families of color placed concerns about safety in interactions with public safety staff as one of their
top three concerns for their family.
1
For our families, these youth and adults with disabilities are our sons, daughters, sisters, and brothers. The TRUST line
staff should be trained and able to safely assist a wider range of disabilities than just those who have mental health
challenges. We ask for a sixty day delay to allow city staff time to meet with and consider the needs of the large and
diverse disability population in San Jose.
In partnership,
[name removed]
Executive Director
PHP "Parents Helping Parents"
[phone removed] ext 153
For news and information to help your family, follow PHP on social media:
Parents Helping Parents (PHP) is a nonprofit organization that provides information, training, individual assistance, and
resources. PHP is not a law firm or legal service agency, and as such, the information contained in this email or in phone
conversations is provided for the purpose of informing the review, but should not be considered legal advice. For legal
advice, you should consult an attorney.
2

comments.item_title: Options for Expanding Alternative Response and Co-Response Programs to 911 Calls for Service. - DEFERRED
comments.subject: PSFSS Item 3: Do NOT accept the “Options for Expanding Alternative Response and Co-Response Programs to
comments.text:
To: PSFSS Chair Jimenez, Vice Chair Doan, Vice Mayor Kamei,
Councilmember Batra and Councilmember Torres
From: Showing Up for Racial Justice Santa Clara County
Subject: Item 3: Do NOT accept the “Options for Expanding Alternative
Response and Co-Response Programs to 911 Calls for Service” report
Date: October 17 2024
[name removed], representing hundreds of SJ residents, is writing to
ask that you defer accepting the “Options for Expanding Alternative Response
and Co-Response Programs to 911 Calls for Service” report and that you
instead direct city staff to return in 60 days with:
1.
Updated recommendations for additional alternative response options to
explore.
2.
An official, written response from the California Department of Health
Care Services as to the legality of funding TRUST with Opioid Settlement
Funds.
We are thankful for the city’s exploratory investment in a 40 hour/week TRUST
field team as well as its pilot investigation of transferring 911 calls to 988 –
these are a good start and we expect to see expansion of both approaches in
the next budget cycle. And we appreciate the comprehensive analysis that city
staff did last year to identify categories of calls that could be directed to more
appropriate responders than police. It is the response to those findings that
remains inadequate. We also take issue with today’s report in several
important ways.
The report itself found that members of disabled communities and their
representatives prefer alternative response programs over co-response
programs that include law enforcement. Yet the report focuses heavily on
“same old, same old” police responses, like CIT, PERT and MCAT. For
example, the report cheerleads for SJPD’s Crisis Intervention Training (CIT),
even though the California Reporting Project Investigation found that not only
did the introduction of CIT not reduce rates of injury and death for people with
disabilities in encounters, but in fact harm actually increased after CIT was
adopted. Why is a report that is supposed to be about expanding alternative
response spending so many words on CIT, a police-only response, in the first
place?
The report also spends pages reviewing co-response both in our county and
other regions, even though it is a less effective, more expensive and more
harmful approach and even though those most directly harmed by co-response
told the city very clearly that non-police response is the option that will reduce
harm. Furthermore, there are two pending lawsuits in Oregon and Washington
D.C. that argue that police response to behavioral health crises is a violation of
the Americans with Disabilities Act, because it discriminates against people
with invisible disabilities. We send EMTs and paramedics to crises
experienced by people with physical disabilities. We don’t expect police to treat
a broken leg; why would we expect them to treat a mental health crisis?
We do not understand why this report focused so heavily on police and co-
response, when the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services
Administration’s national guidelines for behavioral health crisis
response recommend that mobile crisis teams should incorporate peers but
avoid law enforcement accompaniment (except in special circumstances). Los
Angeles’s groundbreaking expansion of mobile crisis response follows this
model and Chicago recently chose to abandon co-response models. As noted
in the LA report (p. 35), “Co-responder teams have demonstrated over time
to be significantly more costly, while not as effective, as civilian teams that
are comprised of a BH clinician and a peer support specialist.”
The report itself acknowledges that lives are at stake: “Recent national data
indicates that people with serious mental health conditions constitute a
statistically significant percentage of suspects injured in police interaction and
involved in use-of-force cases. For example, a recent national study found that
people with mental health conditions are 11.6 times more likely to experience
police use of force, and 10.7 times more likely to experience police-related
injury than those unaffected by mental health conditions. Mental health
conditions often accompany other disabilities, such as autism, and when
accompanied with other structural social
identities – such as race or socioeconomic status – the compounding
intersection of these conditions and identities can lead to higher rates of
victimization.”
Given that this is the case, the report needs to provide more research on non-
police response models and chart a path forwarding to expanding those
models. We do appreciate the report’s recommendation to continue expansion
of the TRUST program in San Jose. However, we believe that the city attorney
is mistaken about the potential use of opioid settlement funds for expanding the
TRUST program. This summer we met directly with staff from the California
Department of Health Care Services (DHCS) to get a deeper understanding of
how opioid settlement funds can be spent. In that meeting, we learned that
crisis response for substance abuse and behavioral health is typically an
allowable use. However, we don’t expect you to take our word for it, which is
why we are asking for an official, written response from the California
Department of Health Care Services as to the legality of funding TRUST with
Opioid Settlement Funds.
In February, the City Council directed staff to explore the following:
Potential models for alternative response and co-response for incidents
involving individuals with a disability
Alternative response models for welfare checks, disturbances, suspicious
circumstances, and trespassing calls involving mental health issues or
unhoused individuals
Potential models that include partner organizations as a co-response with
police to domestic violence calls
This report largely fails to deliver on those requests. The second bullet point
seems to have been ignored entirely. The first and third bullet points don’t take
seriously the real alternative responses that community members want.
The report also notes that non-police response is a racial justice issue: “Many
community members and advocates also supported prioritizing further
investment and resources in alternative response and community-based
programs over co-response programs, as alternative team response can create
more equitable outcomes for communities of color and others
disproportionately impacted by the criminal justice system.”
We are nearing the end of 2024. In response to the racial justice uprisings of
2020, the San Jose City Council made a commitment and promise to re-
imagine public safety. Dozens of impacted community members met for over a
year to develop over 80 recommendations in the city-funded Re-Imagining
Public Safety process. And four years later, the Council has implemented
almost NONE of those recommendations. Racial justice isn’t a fad. It should
be one of the core goals of a city council in a city as richly diverse as San
Jose. If the promise to re-imagine public safety wasn’t just empty virtue-
signaling, if your commitment to racial justice is strong and ongoing, if you
believe that our city should be safe for ALL its residents and most especially
those vulnerable to police violence, you cannot be satisfied with the report
delivered to you this week.
Sincerely,
The members of Showing Up for [name removed]
sources.

comments.text:
Honorable Mayor and City Council,
RE: Council Agenda1/28/25; File 25-054, Item 2.16

1am writing to support the staff recommendation as well as the memo from Mayor Mahan, and Councilmembers Kamei,
Foley and Cohen. The memo recommends allowing any affordable housing developer to use any bond issuer approved by
the State of California. Currently the city requires the city of San Jose to be the bond issuer.

Over the last 35 years, The Core Companies has developed over 5,000 affordable apartments with the vast majority in the
city of San Jose. Most of our projects rely on tax exempt bonds and recently, many of our projects have relied on recycled
bonds. When not in San Jose, we typically work with bond issuers like CalHFA, CSCDA or CFMA. These organizations
specialize in servicing affordable housing projects and are currently faster, more efficient and more cost effective than
working with the City of San Jose as the issuer. In addition, currently the State program incents affordable developers to
utilize recycled bonds however the city of San Jose is unable to provide recycled bonds. As such, we must work through
an extensive process with staff to pursue an exception to council.

This action will enable an under-staffed Housing Department to focus its resources directly on housing and not on bond
policy or process. In addition, it will enable the Department of Finance to focus the workload of its staff. And finally, it
will help affordable developments in San Jose be more competitive when competing for Tax Exempt bonds and Tax Credits
with CDLAC. This is a great example of addition by subtraction.

Sincerely,

comments.text:
To whom it may concern,

| am pleased to be writing this letter in support of Jahmal Williams for District 3 City Council Member. | first met
Jahmal when he was hired to initiate our Early Support program at San Jose State University in 2014. Since
then, I've seen Jahmal in a number of different situations around the university and have had numerous
personal conversations with him about the downtown community. He was very intentional about choosing
homes in the area. As a resident of downtown San Jose for over the last 25 years, this is very important to me.

While I cannot speak for SJSU as an institution, | can say that Jahmal is one of those rare individuals where it
feels like almost everyone who has the opportunity to interact with him speaks about him in high regards and
respects him. Jahmal really listens to people and collaborates to make things happen. | have seen him
essentially build up at least 4 different programs in the last 10 years. These programs always found a way to
support students who are marginalized and use their own strengths and talents to create a better environment.
He inspired people to excel and be the best they could be for themselves and for their communities. He was
able to relate to students, colleagues, and upper administration.

One of the aspects that | most appreciated was that when he had a vision, he made it happen. An example of
this is when he convinced us to begin an Undergraduate Research Opportunity Program (UROP). This is
something that he had experienced and saw the usefulness of it while he was in college and he knew that it
opened up doors for students who may not normally have these opportunities. He did the networking and the
work to persuade people that this would be a good thing at SUSU. It started out small with a cohort of 12
students and 10 faculty and last I heard it is now up to serving 70 students and 35 faculty mentors,

Besides building programs that Jahmal is familiar with, he can build a program that he doesn't initially know a lot
about. He did that with our Early Support program. When Jahmal was first hired, he was asked to research
and develop a way to be more proactive in supporting our students, He reviewed a number of programs across
the country and read the research on what was happening and then put together recommendations about what
should happen. Ultimately, these recommendations were accepted and the first SJSU Early Support program
was born.

Jahmal has been an asset in many other ways. Particularly with how flexible he has been and what he is willing
to do to make the environment around him work. While he was setting up the Early Support Program and
UROP, we had some challenges with staff turnover. Jahmal was asked to take on roles and responsibilities in
addition to the two main programs that he was overseeing. He did so without hesitancy because he knew this
was the best way to support the students and to be a team player so that we were all sharing in the burden. It
has always been amazing to me that while he was doing all of this at work, Jahmal continued to be involved in
his local community sitting on various boards and working to not only enhance SJSU, but also San Jose by
being involved with local businesses and supporting their development.

comments.subject: Item 3.5 - Interim Appointment to Council District 3 and Majority Rule
comments.text:
Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council:

Thank you for voting to conduct a special election for District 3 and for choosing to appoint a new
representative during the interim period. District 3 residents win when democracy wins.

Carl Salas is an excellent candidate for the interim appointment and I hope that you appoint him. I have
known Carl and Marianne Salas for almost 40 years. They are both long-time District 3 residents,
committed to making San Jose better.

They have worked to improve the Campus Community and the greater downtown through volunteer efforts
as well as personal investment. With Carl's energy and Marianne's drive, District 3 will be well served.

Carl has volunteered on many projects, directed clean-ups of Guadalupe River Park and served on the
Guadalupe River Park Conservancy Board. He has led community work through the Rotary. He has high
standards of ethics and has always put others first. His service to the community is unmatched. With his
business experience, community service, his ability to bring people together and his infectious enthusiasm,

Carl will be an excellent interim councilmember

ine Last Thing: The Chi r Mani Majority Rule in the Appointment’

The City Charter is clear that in appointing an interim councilmember, majority rule applies. Section 410 of
Charter unambiguously states:

"If, for any reason, a vacancy, as defined by Charter Section 409, occurs in the office of Mayor or
Council member, the Council shall either fill the vacancy by appointment by a majority of its
remaining members, or call an election for the purpose of filling such vacancy.

This Charter provision confers an important right to the residents of District 3. It prevents a small minority
of the council from blocking the appointment of their councilmember. On November 19th, the Council
voted, contrary to the Charter, to require a two-thirds super-majority for the approval of the interim
councilmember, rather than the majority approval mandated by the Charter. That supermajority vote
grants power to three members of the Council to block the majority appointment of the interim
councilmember.

That rule is contrary to the Charter and is fundamentally undemocratic, giving disproportionate power to
the few and forsaking the approval of a majority.

I appreciate that the motive for this rule was to strive for a consensus pick. But elections of individuals, as
well as the appointment of councilmembers under the Charter, is based on majority rule, not the
empowerment of a council minority.

Please follow the mandate in the Charter and drop the super-majority rule that was recently adopted and
let the majority rule, not the minority. Failure to do so, will cast a cloud on the interim appointment.

Thank you.

[name removed]
[name removed], District 3

Hello,

Celine

January 27, 2025
San Jose Mayor and City Council
200 East Santa Clara Street
San José, CA 95113
Re: Letter of Support for Jahmal Williams (Item #3.5)
Dear Mayor Mahan and Councilmembers,
My name is Céline DinhJanelle. I am a D3 resident, nonprofit attorney, and mother. I write to
enthusiastically recommend Jahmal Williams for the District 3 Councilmember Interim
Appointment.
I know Jahmal in his capacity as a neighbor and loving father. In his personal life, Jahmal
brings together neighbors and community members, builds bridges, and encourages
relationships between people. He is a natural connector.
Jahmal also is beloved community leader, with deep roots in San Jose. He holds multiple
leadership positions in a variety of local institutions – Director of Advocacy for Racial Justice at
San Jose State University, Co-Chair of the Black Leadership Kitchen Cabinet of Silicon Valley,
Board Member of SOMOS Mayfair, and more. His broad experience working with the San Jose
community, and his background in clinical therapy, DEI, advocacy, and community and
government relations work, makes him an adept leader, excellent listener, and creative problem
solver.
In the precise moment – given all that is happening nationally and locally – San Jose needs
someone like Jahmal to apply his broad experience and vision of equity for San Jose. I urge
you to appoint Jahmal as the District 3 Interim Councilmember. Thank you.
Sincerely,
Céline DinhJanelle
D3 Resident

comments.item_title: Interim Appointment to Council District 3. - TO BE HEARD LAST
comments.subject: Agenda item 3.5 public commment
comments.text:
Attached is public comment
sent fi tori

Reasonable accommodations are a legal right, not a privilege.
Denying them violates the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA),
California law, and constitutional principles of equality and fairness.
Public entities have a duty to ensure all individuals, including those
with disabilities, have equal access to services and opportunities.
Failure to do so amounts to discrimination, which the law prohibits.
When an accommodation request is denied—whether due to
ignorance of the law or failure to engage in the required interactive
process—it reflects a failure of responsibility. Ignorance is not an
excuse; public officials are obligated to know and comply with the
law, and to take action when a need for accommodation is raised.
I call on the city to act immediately. First, engage in a fair process to
assess and fulfill reasonable accommodation requests. Second,
ensure proper training for officials to prevent further violations of
disability rights. Lastly, address and correct any existing failures in
the system to prevent ongoing discrimination.
This is about more than compliance; it is about justice, dignity, and
equal rights for all. By fulfilling its obligations, the city can show
leadership, protect civil rights, and uphold the principles of fairness
and inclusion. Everyone deserves the opportunity to participate fully
in public life, and it is the city’s duty to ensure this happens. Thank
you.

comments.item_title: Interim Appointment to Council District 3. - TO BE HEARD LAST
comments.subject: Re appointment of Mr. Jahmal Williams to D3 council seat
comments.text:
Dear members of the San Jose city council,

We would like to highly recommend and enthusiastically endorse Jahmal Williams for the position of interim D3 council
person. We look forward to working with him in that position because San Jose Japantown needs him there.

We have known Jahmal for several years in the context of his concern for and leadership on behalf of vulnerable youth
and marginalized communities in San Jose. We deeply share these concerns. We also know that he holds responsible
positions, not only in his professional position at San Jose State University but in the community as the chairperson of the
Black Leadership Kitchen Cabinet, which plays a significant and trusted role in the welfare and political leadership of the
historic Black community in San Jose.

Jahmal is someone who has a love for and affinity for something close to our hearts and that is the welfare of the San Jose
Japantown community. He understands the deep significance of Japantown, it’s history, the role that the physical
community plays in the collective life of the broader, county-wide Japanese American community, and he understands the
complexities of that history which go beyond concepts of “diversity” and which embrace Heinlenville Chinatown,
Pinoytown, and an historic Black community along with Japantown in what was once a red-lined area of San Jose.

We feel strongly that, as a family man raising young children in D3, Jahmal naturally understands the concerns that San
Jose Japantown remain a small town neighborhood with a thriving, inclusive, friendly commercial and community life.
We know that he is someone who has an appreciation for preservation issues and sustainability issues that we face in San
Jose Japantown, too.

Sincerely yours,
[name removed], long-time D3 residents and active volunteers in the San Jose Japantown community.

January 27, 2025

Mayor and City Council,

As someone who has worked in District 3 with local residents for over two decades, | believe
Jamal Williams would make an exemplary interim Councilmember for this District.

| first witnessed his extraordinary leadership skills coalescing diverse constituencies in the
Reimagining Public Safety Community Advisory Committee, as he helped forge consensus and
clarity on complex public policy concerns. He not only brought his personal experience and
perspective to the process, but connected with others through curiosity and creativity.

Mr. Williams has been a catalyst in the growth, development and influence of the Black
Leadership Kitchen Cabinet which has played an increasingly critical role in articulating the
challenges and priorities of the Black community in San Jose. In his professional role at San Jose
State University, Mr. Williams has spearheaded efforts to bring resources, expertise, and
inspiration to not only the campus community but the wider region. His efforts to engage and
connect community-based organizations with the university on complex issues such as housing,
public safety and racial equity speaks to the inclusive approach that would enrich the San Jose

concerns of young people are included in key conversations on issues affecting everyone in our
downtown community.

1am confident that Jamal Williams would be an exemplary appointment to the City Council
during this transition period and would bring his patient, curious, and inclusive approach,
network of existing relationships with key organizations and downtown residents, and warm

demeanor to the Council and to District 3 residents.

Sincerely,

comments.text:
I have reviewed the memorandum and presentation attachments for this City Council meeting and working
session. | am a property owner in District 3. | am working through issues with Trees and Sidewalks dept.
concerning street drainage in front of our property. As you know Code calls for property owner to be
responsible to keep the sidewalk curb/gutter and trees maintained, And that much we have done and paid for ,
for our property. There remains a failure to drain surface storm water to a drainage inlet at the corner
downstream from us. So a large puddle encompassing all of our curb frontage occurs when it rains. The
blockage is due to tree roots that uplift the street surface adjacent to the curb on the downstream property.

The specific codes covering this were not in the presentation so I asking:

1.) Is this the proper forum to address this?

2.) Who in CSJ can we talk to in order to work on resolution. We have a conversation going with Trees and
Sidewalks but have only reached tentative resolution based on minor curb repairs that do not address
gutter/street surface drainage. T&S tells me that this drainage issue is not in their criteria. We feel we have
talked it out with T&S and we could use a liaison with CSJ to reach a mutually beneficial solution.

3.) How can CSJ and citizens work together to resolve issues such as this and do our best to maintain safe, clean
streets. We are willing to work on solutions and pitch in more than our customary fair share. We currently clean
tree debris and other debris from the street and sidewalk manually because street sweeper avoids this area
because tree roots and uplifted pavement are in the way.

I would like to address the city council tomorrow at the meeting, see you there.

Thank you, Bill coker

comments.item_title: Code Enforcement Operations Study Session
comments.subject: Public Comment - Code Enforcement Operations Study Session - 1/21/2025 - File 25-065
comments.text:
| would like to know what PBCE and DOT staff are empowered to do (or what Council could empower them to
do) when a derelict building on private property is endangering safety along public transportation rights-of-
way such as sidewalks, bike lanes, and transit stops.

This fall, city staff were finally able to re-open the sidewalk adjacent to the burned Lawrence Hotel, on the
north side of E San Fernando St between S 3rd St and S 2nd St. I greatly appreciate that this was able to be
done. What steps needed to be taken in order to get the scaffolding built and the sidewalk re-opened?

The sidewalk had been fenced off for nearly four years. What was the largest source of the long delay, and
what could have been done to allow that to have happened in a period of weeks or months, rather than
years? Is there a new process in place to allow this to happen quicker next time?

What are PBCE and DOT empowered to do (or what could Council empower them to do) to enhance safety
and accessibility along public transportation rights-of-way in situations like this. For example:

* Does the city have authority to perform emergency work on the edge of the private property, with or
without the permission of the property owner, if the property owner is refusing to do such work
themselves in a timely manner? And if the city can do that, can it also sue the private property owner to
recover the expenses of that work?

* Can DOT use temporary materials (eg. cones, plastic posts) to shift/reallocate space within the right-of-
way, allowing pedestrians to have a safe path of travel around the obstruction? For example, can DOT
use cones or plastic posts to temporarily remove some parking or remove/narrow some car travel lanes,
in order to make room to shift the bikeways and "sidewalks"? And can DOT add temporary curb ramps
(like those in San Pedro Square) to allow ADA access in and out of the impromptu walking path?

© Do DOT, Code Enforcement, or SJPD have any enhanced enforcement powers in cases where the public
transportation right-of-way is impeded or endangered by a derelict building?

¢ Is there any action that Council can take to empower city staff in the above ways?

What actions can be taken, and by what department(s), when private property is being stored indefinitely in a
transportation right-of-way? An example that comes to my mind is a business's dumpster that seems to be
stored in a bike lane 24/7/365. Which department is responsible for addressing such an issue, and how
quickly could such an issue be resolved?

Slides 6 indicates which departments are responsible for "Maintenance and Preservation of the Built
Environment" on private vs. public property. But when private property creates a physical impact on public
right-of-way, is there a straightforward, unambiguous, and timely procedure for ensuring that at least one
department is actively working on resolving the incident? Or are there any difficulties with such incidents
falling through the cracks, or bouncing back-and-forth between departments?

Thanks,

[name removed] (speaking on my own behalf)
District 3, Japantown, 95112

comments.text:
ict7 @sanjoseca.gov>; Dominic Dursa

Attached is the Japantown Business Association's comment concerning blighted buildings in our community, and its
connection to the Code Enforcement Operations Study Session. Thank you!

Regards,
[name removed]

President, Japantown Business Association (JBA)

JBA web: japantownsanjose.org
www. jtown.or

JAPANTOWN BUSINESS ASSOCIATION
January 20, 2025
City of San Jose City Council
Attn: Planning, Building & Code Enforcement
200 E. Santa Clara Street
San Jose, CA 95113
RE: Planning, Building, and Code Enforcement (PBCE) Code Enforcement Operations Study
Session
Dear Mayor Mahan and Honorable Councilmembers,
Downtown is not the only San Jose district facing pervasive blight. "What's up with the busted buildings in
Japantown," is a phrase I've been asked far too many times.
In just over two blocks of our Business Improvement District, we have ten boarded-up or vacant
commercial and residential buildings. All but two are listed on the City of San Jose's Historic Resources
Inventory and blighted in part due to restrictive historic mandates. There are over 125 Japantown parcels in
the Historic Resources Inventory, and virtually none of our property owners are aware of it.
Complex dialogue between San Jose's Historic Landmarks Commission, Code Enforcement, Planning, and
Building Departments, as well as unclear distinctions between local and state building regulations for
historic properties compounds the issue.
The term "blighted" has historically been used to designate properties and land for government-backed
seizure under eminent domain and has racist implications. I am using this language in its contemporary
form to call out the results of prohibitive measures that prevented our community from maintaining its
properties.
• Three buildings on Taylor Street have been boarded up for over 2 years and underwent a $25K review
by a City-approved Historic Resources Consultant and multiple checks by the aforementioned City
departments. In that time, thieves have stripped one building entirely of its electrical wires, including the
service panel, and squatters have attempted to set fire to it three times.
• One residential home on N. 5th Street has been vacant and condemned for over 20 years. I have
personally boarded it up twice on behalf of its senior owners.
• Two other residential homes on N. 4th Street stand in the way of a new Dharma Center and preschool
for the Buddhist Church. My great-uncle owned one home and has the family's blessing to be
demolished. It's been boarded up for over 20 years.
• A two-story brick building on N. 6th Street requires more than $1M in seismic retrofitting. It has
changed ownership three times in fifteen years, has been vacant for over twenty, and recently had a
piece of the structure fall from the second story onto the public sidewalk. The interior second floor has
collapsed, and the building has also caught fire. Investors sell the building when they realize it is
financially unsustainable to retrofit.
• The Kawakami House, moved to make room for the Japanese American Museum of San Jose in 2006,
remains boarded up, frequently invaded by squatters, and without the substantial monetary investment
– estimated to be $2.5M – for renovation.
• The Mineta House, the former childhood home of Japantown's own Norman Mineta, has exceeded its
renovation budget as its new owners, one of Japantown's leading churches, discovered that their plans
needed to meet historic requirements.
565 N. 6th Street, Suite G. San Jose, CA 95112. phone [phone removed]. [email removed]
These parcels are not owned by irresponsible offshore entities but almost entirely by local families and
nonprofits. The requirements meant to protect our history are causing the opposite – bankrupting our
families, damaging our nonprofits, and exposing our community to theft, squatters, fire, physical harm, and
vulnerability to corporate gentrification or eminent domain.
As someone who is 5th generation Japantown and whose grandparents and great-grandparents, aunts,
and uncles were incarcerated during WWII, I understand the importance of our own history. Our family also
moved and restored our historic 19th Century Italianate Victorian home and rebuilt our Grandfather's
Japantown gas station as a coffee shop. We fully understand the financial and logistical challenges of
landmark renovation.
We want to preserve our legacy, history, and places, but it's time for the City to allow us the permission,
flexibility, and authority to determine our future. We need help to achieve a reasonable balance between
preservation and growth that strengthens our historically marginalized, ethnic community.
We appreciate any and all consideration the City Council, Code Enforcement, Historic Landmarks
Commission, and Historic Preservation Officer may provide us.
Best,
[name removed]
President, Japantown Business Association
565 N. 6th Street, Suite G. San Jose, CA 95112. phone [phone removed]. [email removed]

comments.item_title: Resolution Reaffirming the City’s Commitment to Preserving the Safety and Dignity of all its Residents, Regardless of National Origin or Legal Status.
comments.subject: Item C-2 Jan. 15 Rules Committee: Support for Immigrant Protection Memo
comments.text:
Clerk San Jose Councilmember,
Dear Rules Committee Members,
As a resident of San Jose and as a first generation Latine, I am writing to express my strong
support for the memo proposed by Councilmembers Ortiz, Campos, Cohen, and Candelas,
which outlines critical actions to protect our city's residents from the harmful policies of
the incoming presidential administration.
San Jose has always been a city that values its diversity and stands with its immigrant
communities, who are essential to our city. The threats posed by mass deportation policies
and heightened immigration enforcement risk tearing families apart, spreading fear, and
undermining public safety.
The steps outlined in this memo - strengthening the Rapid Response Network, providing
legal and support services, and reaffirming our sanctuary city policies - are vital to
preserving the trust, safety, and dignity of all San Jose residents. By passing this memo, the
City Council can send a clear message that San Jose will remain a place where all
communities are valued and protected.
I urge you to pass this memo to safeguard our city's future.
Thank you for your leadership and commitment to ensuring that San Jose remains a
welcoming and inclusive city for everyone.
Sincerely
[name removed]s
[name removed]s

Clerk San Jose Councilmember,
Dear Rules Committee Members,

As a resident of District 6 and a member of Showing Up for Racial Justice Santa Clara
County, | am writing to express my strong support for the memo proposed by
Councilmembers Ortiz, Campos, Cohen, and Candelas, which outlines critical actions to
protect our city’s residents from the harmful policies of the incoming presidential
administration.

San José has always been a city that values its diversity and stands with its immigrant
communities, who are essential to our city. The threats posed by mass deportation policies
and heightened immigration enforcement risk tearing families apart, spreading fear, and
undermining public safety.

The steps outlined in this memo — strengthening the Rapid Response Network, providing
legal and support services, and reaffirming our sanctuary city policies — are vital to
preserving the trust, safety, and dignity of all San José residents. By passing this memo, the
City Council can send a clear message that San José will remain a place where all
communities are valued and protected.

| urge you to pass this memo to safeguard our city’s future.

Thank you for your leadership and commitment to ensuring that San José remains a
welcoming and inclusive city for everyone.

Sincerely
{FirstName}

comments.subject: Item C-2 Jan. 15 Rules Committee: Support for Immigrant Protection Memo
comments.text:
Clerk San Jose Councilmember,
Dear Rules Committee Members,

My name is [name removed], and | work in San José, where | am dedicated to supporting our
community, particularly individuals with developmental disabilities. | am writing to express
my strong support for the memo proposed by Councilmembers Ortiz, Campos, Cohen,
and Candelas, which outlines crucial actions to protect our city’s residents from the
harmful policies of the incoming presidential administration.

San José has long been a place of refuge for immigrants seeking safety, stability, and
opportunity. Among those immigrants, many families of individuals with developmental
disabilities rely heavily on the supportive resources our city provides, including housing,
healthcare, and social services. For these families, especially those who are undocumented
or have uncertain immigration status, San José represents more than just a city—it is a
lifeline, offering a place where they can rebuild their lives, access the care they need, and
seek safety and stability for their loved ones.

Housing is a cornerstone of this stability. Families, particularly those navigating the
compounded challenges of disability and immigration status, face immense pressure in
securing housing. Disrupting these families through deportation and immigration
enforcement puts them at even greater risk of homelessness and isolation, leaving

individuals with developmental disabilities without the essential medical and emotional
support systems they need to thrive.

San José is home to a diverse immigrant population, many of whom are in urgent need of
accessible housing and supportive services. We must remain open, kind, and human in our
approach, ensuring that all immigrants, especially those with disabilities or navigating
precarious legal status, feel welcomed and supported in our city. The steps outlined in this
memo—strengthening the Rapid Response Network, providing legal and support services,
and reaffirming our sanctuary city policies—are vital to ensuring these families and
individuals receive the protection and stability they deserve.

| urge you to pass this memo to protect immigrant families and ensure San José continues
to be a city that embodies compassion and inclusion. Your leadership is essential in
preserving the dignity, safety, and stability of our most vulnerable residents, ensuring that
all families, including those with members with developmental disabilities, can thrive in a
secure and supportive environment.

Thank you for your dedication to creating a better future for all who call San José home.

Sincerely,
[name removed]

[name removed]

comments.subject: Jan. 15 Rules Committee Item C-2: Solidarity with our immigrant communities
comments.text:
Clerk San Jose Councilmember,
Dear Rules Committee Members,

| am writing in solidarity with our immigrant communities to urge you to support the
memo proposed by Councilmembers Ortiz, Campos, Cohen, and Candelas. It is vital that
our city do everything in its power to protect our immigrant families from the destructive
policies of the incoming presidential administration.

San José is one of the most diverse large cities in the United States, with recent census
data showing that nearly 42% of our residents were born in other countries. Our diversity
enriches the character and culture of our city and strengthens all of our communities. The
particular threats posed by the Trump administration to launch mass deportation
campaigns are horrifying and risk tearing our families and communities apart.

This memo is an important first step for San José to reaffirm its commitment to all our
residents by strengthening the Rapid Response Network, providing legal and support
services, and affirming our sanctuary city policies. No one should live in fear in our city.
Please support this memo and safeguard our communities.

Thank you for your leadership and commitment to ensuring that San José remains a
welcoming and inclusive city for all.

Sincerely,
[name removed]
[name removed]

Clerk San Jose Councilmember,

Dear Rules Committee Members,

As a resident of San José, | am writing to express my strong support for the memo
proposed by Councilmembers Ortiz, Campos, Cohen, and Candelas, which outlines critical
actions to protect our city’s residents from the harmful policies of the incoming
presidential administration.

San José has always been a city that values its diversity and stands with its immigrant
communities, who are essential to our city. The threats posed by mass deportation policies
and heightened immigration enforcement risk tearing families apart, spreading fear, and
undermining public safety.

The steps outlined in this memo — strengthening the Rapid Response Network, providing
legal and support services, and reaffirming our sanctuary city policies — are vital to
preserving the trust, safety, and dignity of all San José residents. By passing this memo, the
City Council can send a clear message that San José will remain a place where all
communities are valued and protected.

| urge you to pass this memo to safeguard our city’s future.

Thank you for your leadership and commitment to ensuring that San José remains a
welcoming and inclusive city for everyone.

Sincerely

{FirstName}

[name removed]

San Jose, California 95123

Re: Council Agenda: 2/4/2025; File: 25-081; Item: 2.9
Dear Members of the San José City Council,
My name is Alberto Camacho and I am a proud child of immigrants and East Side resident. I’ve
lived nearly my entire life on McKee and White, surrounded and nurtured by neighbors from all
over the world —amazing people who have informed the man I am today. My parents arrived
here at different points of their lives, with both seeking el sueño Americano. While in search of
that dream, they navigated throughout an entirely foreign system, often afraid and anxious, but
deep down they knew their community would support them and so would the people in power
whose families also came in search of a dream.
I write to you all urging to pass the motion that supports our immigrant communities here in San
José, a city that’s known for its tenderness, empathy, and strong sense of community. As an
educator within the East Side of San José, I make sure to replicate those traits that San José has
shown my parents and community. My students, their families, my family, and me hope that you
vote to protect those who so often speak, but are often left unheard.
Throughout these couple of weeks, I have had students share with me their fear, their anger, and
desperation as they go day by day living with an uncertainty that impacts their day to day.
Fortunately, the Rapid Response Network is available to support them with legal assistance and
some sort of stability. I know for a fact that without the support of the Rapid Response Network,
many the families I serve would fall through the cracks. I want to reiterate my hope that you vote
in favor of the motion that seeks to support nuestra gente.
On behalf of my parents, the community I serve, and myself, I thank you for your time and
careful consideration to protect our families from vengeful acts rooted in hate and racism.
Best,
[name removed]

Dear Members of the San José City Council,
My name is [name removed], proud daughter of immigrants, who was born and raised in east side
San Jose. As a first generation student, educator, and resident of district 5, I have seen the
invaluable worth and contributions of our immigrant community first hand. In an intercambio of
cultures from all over the world, this community has woven together a story of courage, empathy,
cariño, perseverance, and hope that makes the heartbeat of San Jose. Testimonies of people like
my parents show the valor it takes to entrust a place and people unfamiliar to oneself, seeking out
a better life for their and future generations. Many like them arrive in this country with a selfless
heart and gratitude to sought out opportunities. Today, the presidential administration has
generated a state of fear and anxiety, threatening essential rights and protections for immigrants.
I urge you all to take a stance in protecting the civic and cultural rights of immigrant
communities by passing the motion in item 2.9. Our collective well being is dependent on the
safety, inclusion, and upliftment of immigrant communities in all places of learning, work, and
leisure. As a former elementary educator, I have witnessed the sacrifices alongside the joys of
families constructing a world better than our present for future generations. These parents and
caregivers give meaning to the concept: “Planting seeds for trees we may never get to witness”.
Moving with empathy, tenacity, and a selfless heart, immigrant communities have been the
keepers of San Jose’s freedom dreams for many generations. Nuestro barrio es vibrante por el
color, la música y cultura de estos artistas - artists who use what tools they have to multiply the
life around them.
By expanding the Rapid Response Network alongside legal assistance and services, eastside San
Jose does right by our indebtment to immeasurable contributions from immigrant communities.
San Jose is to be more than a sanctuary – a place where my neighbors, students, and comrades
are not halted to fear – where we take care of one another’s holistic wellbeing beyond survival.
Thank you for your attention to this critical issue, and for your continued leadership in making
San José a place where all people are treated with respect and dignity.

comments.subject: Public Comment Letter for Inclusion on Proclamation to Protect All Immigrants (Item 2.9) of 2/4/25 City
comments.text:
Council Meeting
Hello, please see attached, and let us know you received it, thank you! - Raj

February 3, 2025
To: San Jose City Council
From: Silicon Valley De-Bug
Re: Including “All” Immigrants in Proclamation (Item 2.9 of February 4th Council Meeting)
As an organization that advocates for immigrant rights, racial justice, and freedom from the carceral
system -- all of which we see as expressions of the same struggle -- we are calling on the City of San
Jose to revise this proclamation.
San Jose must create an inclusive resolution to stand with all immigrants, not only some. As
currently written, and expressed in media statements by the Mayor - the City of San Jose is
acquiescing to Trump’s anti-immigrant agenda by endorsing the detention and deportation of
immigrant community members who have had contact with the criminal legal system.
The excluding language of “law-abiding” in the resolution is intended to message to the community
that San Jose is willing to sacrifice our fellow community members, our neighbors, our loved ones
simply because of their contact with the criminal legal system. It is the ignorant and false dichotomy
of the “good” versus “bad” immigrant - who is deserving of rights and who is not. San Jose should
be a city that sees through that illusionary and racist frame - and protects all our community
members.
This rubber-stamping of who the city is willing to allow ICE to detain is legally incorrect,
strategically naive, and ultimately counter to our city’s collective values of inclusion.
For one, the criminal legal system is not a proxy for immigration enforcement. A city messaging that
if someone has a criminal record, they are not due the same level of solidarity or protection is
unethical - that the city would codify that into a proclamation that is by definition aspirational, is
abhorrent. This thinking, that the rights of some immigrants should be protected while others
abandoned, only bolsters Trump’s racist and false specter of the “dangerous” immigrants. Plus, in
response to the question of who is being targeted in mass deportation campaigns - the
administration clearly stated all undocumented immigrants are “criminals.” Who the city avails
protections to, and who it does not, is a slippery slope that ultimately leaves all immigrant
communities vulnerable.
There is a key word missing from the title of this proclamation. The word is “all” - that the city of
San Jose is reaffirming the city’s commitment to protecting the rights and safety of “all” immigrant
communities.

comments.text:
all its Residents...
I am writing to oppose item 2.9 “Resolution Reaffirming the City’s Commitment to
Preserving the Safety and Dignity of all its Residents, Regardless of National Origin or
Legal Status.”
I am opposing this resolution because the City of San Jose is contradicting itself as a
“Welcoming City” for it already has another resolution in the book, the so-called
“Resolution 3.8” adopted in 2017, which banned the flag of a foreign nation, Vietnam, in
the City of San Jose. That resolution specifically discriminated against a particular group
of people based on country of origin.
Furthermore, nothing is more unsettling to a lot of people living in San Jose than watching
hundreds of protesters flying flags of foreign nations demanding that American citizens
use their hard-earned tax dollars (proposed under item 2.9) to pay for support services for
those who are here illegally.
If the City is willing to ban a flag of one foreign nation under Resolution 3.8, then why
does it willing to support protesters flying the flags of other foreign nations demanding
that this City treat them with dignity and respect.
I have previously spoken against Resolution 3.8 which specifically targets a certain
immigrant group and makes them “unwelcome” in the City of San Jose. And now the City
wants to adopt another resolution claiming that all immigrants should be treated with
dignity and respect, such action does not make any sense at all.
How can you discriminate against one group of immigrants and then favor other groups
and then call yourself a “Welcoming City”?
The immigrant group affected by Resolution 3.8 are law abiding legal residents and
citizens. They have done no harms, committed no offenses against the City, and yet they
are being targeted because of their national origin. They themselves did not get the same
treatment of respect and dignity that they deserved and adding “insult to injury” they are
being asked to use their tax dollars to fund support services to those who are not even here
legally, flying flags of foreign nations.
The City of San Jose cannot adopt this proposed resolution without addressing the
injustice committed under the previous Resolution 3.8 (2017) targeting the people from
the country of Vietnam and then giving preferential treatments to people from other
countries targeted by ICE under Donald Trump.

comments.item_title: Options for Expanding Alternative Response and Co-Response Programs to 911 Calls for Service.
comments.subject: Feedback: Disability Community Concerns, PSFSS meeting 10/17
comments.text:
Dear City Council Members Jimenez, Doan, Kamei, Torres, and Batra:
I am writing today regarding item (d)3 on the October 17 agenda for the Public Safety, Finance, and Strategic Support
Committee (PSFSS), Options for Expanding Alternative Response and Co-Response Programs to 911 Calls for Service.
Parents Helping Parents is the lead agency in Santa Clara County supporting parents of children with disabilities; each
year over 6,000 county residents are served by PHP.
We ask members of PSFSS to defer accepting the report and direct staff to return within 60 days with updated
recommendations for additional alternative response options to explore TRUST responses to the disability community
beyond mental health disabilities.
Our concern is around Finding #1 and FInding #3:
Finding #1: Finding #1 preference for alternative response The first finding, that members of disabled communities and
their representatives, prefer alternative response programs over co-response programs (with law enforcement), is the
key finding, and all decisions made by city officials should follow from it.
Finding #3: As the staff report details, “Many community members and advocates also supported prioritizing further
investment and resources in alternative response and community-based programs over co-response programs, as
alternative team response can create more equitable outcomes for communities of color and others
disproportionately impacted by the criminal justice system.” (emphasis added). We do agree with the recommendation
to hire more clinicians and others with the skills to communicate with people with particular disabilities, such as those
fluent in American Sign Language.
San José should strive to remove armed officers from as many situations as possible rather than put the onus of safety
on community members, as detailed in several examples from other jurisdictions cited in the staff report.
We would respectfully like to remind committee members that currently 1 in 36 children in our region and our country
are born with autism, and that 20% of the population has disabilities. People of color with disabilities are more at risk
than any other segment of the population when police become involved. In a recent town hall meeting at Parents
Helping Parents, we collected survey responses from families on the top eight public policy priorities for their families: a
full two-thirds of our families of color placed concerns about safety in interactions with public safety staff as one of their
top three concerns for their family.
1
For our families, these youth and adults with disabilities are our sons, daughters, sisters, and brothers. The TRUST line
staff should be trained and able to safely assist a wider range of disabilities than just those who have mental health
challenges. We ask for a sixty day delay to allow city staff time to meet with and consider the needs of the large and
diverse disability population in San Jose.
In partnership,
[name removed]
Executive Director
PHP "Parents Helping Parents"
[phone removed] ext 153
For news and information to help your family, follow PHP on social media:
Parents Helping Parents (PHP) is a nonprofit organization that provides information, training, individual assistance, and
resources. PHP is not a law firm or legal service agency, and as such, the information contained in this email or in phone
conversations is provided for the purpose of informing the review, but should not be considered legal advice. For legal
advice, you should consult an attorney.
2

comments.item_title: Options for Expanding Alternative Response and Co-Response Programs to 911 Calls for Service.
comments.subject: PSFSS Item 3: Do NOT accept the “Options for Expanding Alternative Response and Co-Response Programs to
comments.text:
To: PSFSS Chair Jimenez, Vice Chair Doan, Vice Mayor Kamei,
Councilmember Batra and Councilmember Torres
From: Showing Up for Racial Justice Santa Clara County
Subject: Item 3: Do NOT accept the “Options for Expanding Alternative
Response and Co-Response Programs to 911 Calls for Service” report
Date: October 17 2024
[name removed], representing hundreds of SJ residents, is writing to
ask that you defer accepting the “Options for Expanding Alternative Response
and Co-Response Programs to 911 Calls for Service” report and that you
instead direct city staff to return in 60 days with:
1.
Updated recommendations for additional alternative response options to
explore.
2.
An official, written response from the California Department of Health
Care Services as to the legality of funding TRUST with Opioid Settlement
Funds.
We are thankful for the city’s exploratory investment in a 40 hour/week TRUST
field team as well as its pilot investigation of transferring 911 calls to 988 –
these are a good start and we expect to see expansion of both approaches in
the next budget cycle. And we appreciate the comprehensive analysis that city
staff did last year to identify categories of calls that could be directed to more
appropriate responders than police. It is the response to those findings that
remains inadequate. We also take issue with today’s report in several
important ways.
The report itself found that members of disabled communities and their
representatives prefer alternative response programs over co-response
programs that include law enforcement. Yet the report focuses heavily on
“same old, same old” police responses, like CIT, PERT and MCAT. For
example, the report cheerleads for SJPD’s Crisis Intervention Training (CIT),
even though the California Reporting Project Investigation found that not only
did the introduction of CIT not reduce rates of injury and death for people with
disabilities in encounters, but in fact harm actually increased after CIT was
adopted. Why is a report that is supposed to be about expanding alternative
response spending so many words on CIT, a police-only response, in the first
place?
The report also spends pages reviewing co-response both in our county and
other regions, even though it is a less effective, more expensive and more
harmful approach and even though those most directly harmed by co-response
told the city very clearly that non-police response is the option that will reduce
harm. Furthermore, there are two pending lawsuits in Oregon and Washington
D.C. that argue that police response to behavioral health crises is a violation of
the Americans with Disabilities Act, because it discriminates against people
with invisible disabilities. We send EMTs and paramedics to crises
experienced by people with physical disabilities. We don’t expect police to treat
a broken leg; why would we expect them to treat a mental health crisis?
We do not understand why this report focused so heavily on police and co-
response, when the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services
Administration’s national guidelines for behavioral health crisis
response recommend that mobile crisis teams should incorporate peers but
avoid law enforcement accompaniment (except in special circumstances). Los
Angeles’s groundbreaking expansion of mobile crisis response follows this
model and Chicago recently chose to abandon co-response models. As noted
in the LA report (p. 35), “Co-responder teams have demonstrated over time
to be significantly more costly, while not as effective, as civilian teams that
are comprised of a BH clinician and a peer support specialist.”
The report itself acknowledges that lives are at stake: “Recent national data
indicates that people with serious mental health conditions constitute a
statistically significant percentage of suspects injured in police interaction and
involved in use-of-force cases. For example, a recent national study found that
people with mental health conditions are 11.6 times more likely to experience
police use of force, and 10.7 times more likely to experience police-related
injury than those unaffected by mental health conditions. Mental health
conditions often accompany other disabilities, such as autism, and when
accompanied with other structural social
identities – such as race or socioeconomic status – the compounding
intersection of these conditions and identities can lead to higher rates of
victimization.”
Given that this is the case, the report needs to provide more research on non-
police response models and chart a path forwarding to expanding those
models. We do appreciate the report’s recommendation to continue expansion
of the TRUST program in San Jose. However, we believe that the city attorney
is mistaken about the potential use of opioid settlement funds for expanding the
TRUST program. This summer we met directly with staff from the California
Department of Health Care Services (DHCS) to get a deeper understanding of
how opioid settlement funds can be spent. In that meeting, we learned that
crisis response for substance abuse and behavioral health is typically an
allowable use. However, we don’t expect you to take our word for it, which is
why we are asking for an official, written response from the California
Department of Health Care Services as to the legality of funding TRUST with
Opioid Settlement Funds.
In February, the City Council directed staff to explore the following:
Potential models for alternative response and co-response for incidents
involving individuals with a disability
Alternative response models for welfare checks, disturbances, suspicious
circumstances, and trespassing calls involving mental health issues or
unhoused individuals
Potential models that include partner organizations as a co-response with
police to domestic violence calls
This report largely fails to deliver on those requests. The second bullet point
seems to have been ignored entirely. The first and third bullet points don’t take
seriously the real alternative responses that community members want.
The report also notes that non-police response is a racial justice issue: “Many
community members and advocates also supported prioritizing further
investment and resources in alternative response and community-based
programs over co-response programs, as alternative team response can create
more equitable outcomes for communities of color and others
disproportionately impacted by the criminal justice system.”
We are nearing the end of 2024. In response to the racial justice uprisings of
2020, the San Jose City Council made a commitment and promise to re-
imagine public safety. Dozens of impacted community members met for over a
year to develop over 80 recommendations in the city-funded Re-Imagining
Public Safety process. And four years later, the Council has implemented
almost NONE of those recommendations. Racial justice isn’t a fad. It should
be one of the core goals of a city council in a city as richly diverse as San
Jose. If the promise to re-imagine public safety wasn’t just empty virtue-
signaling, if your commitment to racial justice is strong and ongoing, if you
believe that our city should be safe for ALL its residents and most especially
those vulnerable to police violence, you cannot be satisfied with the report
delivered to you this week.
Sincerely,
The members of Showing Up for [name removed]
sources.

comments.item_title: Terra Verde data center: EIR certification and site development permit
comments.subject: Strongly oppose the Terra Verde data center
comments.text:
Dear Councilmember,

I live in Alviso and I am strongly OPPOSED to the proposed Terra Verde data center off Gold Street. Alviso already sits below sea level and floods — the last thing we need is acres of concrete and a facility drawing millions of gallons for cooling. Who gets the water when there's a drought, us or the servers?

This belongs nowhere near a flood-prone residential community. Please vote no.

[name removed]

comments.item_title: Terra Verde data center: EIR certification and site development permit
comments.subject: data center = more jobs, I support it
comments.text: I know everyone's mad but honestly I SUPPORT the Terra Verde project. North San Jose has empty industrial lots doing nothing. Construction jobs, tax base, and it's an industrial zone — not someone's backyard. We can't say no to everything and then complain about the budget. Build it.

comments.item_title: Terra Verde data center: EIR certification and site development permit
comments.subject: Request for independent environmental review — Terra Verde
comments.text:
Dear Councilmember,

I am a hydrologist and an Alviso resident. I'm not reflexively anti-development, but the Terra Verde EIR appears to understate groundwater and cooling-water demand and does not adequately model cumulative flood impacts. I OPPOSE certification of the EIR as written and request an independent peer review before any vote.

I'm happy to provide technical comments. Thank you.

[name removed], PhD

comments.text: Would lights stay off a month in a wealthy neighborhood? No. The East Side waits because we always wait. I SUPPORT a funded reliability program AND a policy that outage response is equal across the city. This is about fairness.

comments.item_title: Streetlight reliability program and maintenance contract (Story/King corridor)
comments.subject: the solar ones
comments.text: why not solar streetlights on the corridor, then copper theft is pointless and outages dont cascade. im for whatever is most reliable. just do SOMETHING on story rd

comments.item_title: Streetlight reliability program and maintenance contract (Story/King corridor)
comments.subject: my street light has been out for months, forget weeks
comments.text: Everyone's talking about Story and King but my single light around the corner has been out since spring and nobody cares about one light. I support fixing the corridor but please don't forget the individual outages too. Mixed feelings about where the money goes.

comments.item_title: Streetlight reliability program and maintenance contract (Story/King corridor)
comments.subject: our evening services
comments.text: Our congregation meets in the evening near King Road and elderly members are afraid to come in the dark. I SUPPORT emergency lighting restoration. Please help our community gather safely.

comments.item_title: Streetlight reliability program and maintenance contract (Story/King corridor)
comments.subject: AGAINST the vendor's maintenance fees
comments.text: Read the fine print on that smart-light contract — ongoing cloud/software fees for YEARS. I OPPOSE locking the city into vendor fees to make a streetlight turn on. Buy reliable hardware outright and protect the wire. That's it.

comments.item_title: Streetlight reliability program and maintenance contract (Story/King corridor)
comments.subject: small business suffering
comments.text: My shop near Story Rd loses evening customers because people avoid the dark street. I SUPPORT getting the lights back fast. This is costing local businesses real money every night.

comments.item_title: Streetlight reliability program and maintenance contract (Story/King corridor)
comments.subject: I don't live there but
comments.text: I don't live on that corridor but I read about it and I support the city fixing it fast. Basic safety shouldn't depend on your zip code. Fund it.

comments.item_title: Streetlight reliability program and maintenance contract (Story/King corridor)
comments.subject: opposed to blaming PG&E
comments.text: The city keeps blaming PG&E to avoid responsibility. Some of these are city-owned lights. I OPPOSE the finger-pointing. Own it and fix the ones you're responsible for on King Road.

comments.item_title: Streetlight reliability program and maintenance contract (Story/King corridor)
comments.subject: worried about my commute
comments.text: not sure whose fault it is but the whole area is dark and i drive through at 5am. scary. please fix. i'd support funding if that's what it takes.

comments.item_title: Streetlight reliability program and maintenance contract (Story/King corridor)
comments.subject: cut something else to pay for this
comments.text: I SUPPORT restoring the lights but I OPPOSE a new tax or fee for it. Reprioritize the budget you already have. This is a core service — fund it from existing money, not my wallet.

comments.item_title: Streetlight reliability program and maintenance contract (Story/King corridor)
comments.subject: thank you for the temporary towers
comments.text: I saw crews put up a couple of temporary light towers near Story this week — thank you! I SUPPORT making the permanent fix a priority now so they don't come down and leave us dark again. Appreciate the quick interim help.

comments.item_title: Streetlight reliability program and maintenance contract (Story/King corridor)
comments.subject: data on crime please
comments.text: Before funding a big program I'd like to see actual data that the outage increased crime on the corridor. I might support it, but show the evidence. Right now I'm neutral and want facts, not anecdotes.

comments.item_title: Streetlight reliability program and maintenance contract (Story/King corridor)
comments.subject: night photo attached, still dark
comments.text: Two weeks after I first reported it, still dark. Photo attached from last night at the King Rd crosswalk. I oppose how slow this is. Please escalate.

comments.item_title: Pavement maintenance: emergency repair on Alma Avenue and road funding
comments.subject: Giant pothole on Alma Ave — someone will get hurt
comments.text:
Hello,

There is a huge pothole on Alma Avenue just west of the Washington area. It is at least two feet across and deep. I've seen two cyclists nearly thrown off. I've reported it on the app three times since July. Nothing.

I OPPOSE the city's pattern of ignoring the Gardner/Washington streets. Please fix this specific hole now before someone is seriously injured.

comments.subject: that crater on Alma blew my tire
comments.text: The pothole on Alma Ave destroyed my front tire this morning — $220. It's been there for MONTHS. How is this acceptable? I OPPOSE the city's maintenance priorities. I want reimbursement info and I want it filled this week.

comments.item_title: Pavement maintenance: emergency repair on Alma Avenue and road funding
comments.subject: Support a one-time emergency patch for Alma Ave
comments.text:
Dear Councilmember,

Rather than wait for the full repaving queue, I SUPPORT authorizing an emergency same-week patch for the Alma Avenue pothole. It's dangerous now. A proper repave can follow, but please SUPPORT an immediate temporary fix. Thank you.

comments.subject: Alma Avenue pothole — photo attached

comments.item_title: Proactive rental inspection and habitability enforcement
comments.subject: No hot water for 9 days at Cedar Court
comments.text:
Dear Councilmember,

Tenants at Cedar Court Apartments near Tully Road have had NO hot water for nine days. The landlord ignores us. We have children bathing in cold water. I called code enforcement and got a case number but no inspector yet.

I OPPOSE the slow code enforcement response. Please send an inspector and hold the owner accountable.

[name removed]

comments.item_title: Proactive rental inspection and habitability enforcement
comments.subject: cold showers every morning
comments.text: its freezing cold water only at our building off tully. been weeks. management says 'working on it'. nothing. i oppose how the city lets slumlords ignore this. please help us.

comments.item_title: Proactive rental inspection and habitability enforcement
comments.subject: Sin agua caliente en Cedar Court
comments.text:
Buenas noches,

En los apartamentos Cedar Court llevamos más de una semana sin agua caliente. El dueño no responde y mis hijos se bañan con agua fría. Reporté al departamento de código pero no ha venido nadie.

Me opongo a que ignoren a los inquilinos. Por favor manden un inspector pronto. Gracias.

[name removed]

comments.item_title: Proactive rental inspection and habitability enforcement
comments.subject: Support stronger habitability enforcement
comments.text: I SUPPORT the city's proposed proactive rental inspection program. The Cedar Court hot-water mess shows waiting for complaints doesn't work. Inspect regularly and fine bad owners. Please fund it.

comments.item_title: Proactive rental inspection and habitability enforcement
comments.subject: Re: Cedar Court — boiler on order
comments.text:
To the council office,

Regarding complaints about Cedar Court: the central boiler failed and a replacement part is on backorder. We OPPOSE characterizations that we are ignoring tenants and request the city not issue penalties while the repair is in progress. We expect resolution within the week.

Property Management

comments.item_title: Proactive rental inspection and habitability enforcement
comments.subject: it's not just hot water
comments.text: At Cedar Court it's hot water now but also mold in the units and a broken security gate. Main issue is the hot water but the whole place is neglected. I oppose letting this owner off easy. Please do a full inspection.

comments.item_title: Proactive rental inspection and habitability enforcement
comments.subject: careful about overregulating small landlords
comments.text: I sympathize with those tenants, but I'm worried a heavy proactive-inspection mandate will burden small honest landlords with fees for the sins of a few. I'm genuinely torn on the program — target the bad actors, don't blanket everyone.

comments.item_title: Proactive rental inspection and habitability enforcement
comments.subject: Không có nước nóng ở khu căn hộ
comments.text:

Khu căn hộ của chúng tôi gần Tully Road đã mất nước nóng hơn một tuần. Chủ nhà không sửa. Trời lạnh mà con tôi phải tắm nước lạnh. Tôi đã gọi báo nhưng chưa ai đến.

Tôi mong thành phố buộc chủ nhà sửa chữa và bảo vệ người thuê nhà. Cảm ơn quý vị.

comments.item_title: Proactive rental inspection and habitability enforcement
comments.subject: fine them per day
comments.text: If a landlord leaves tenants without hot water for a week there should be a daily fine that actually hurts. I SUPPORT steep habitability penalties. Cold water in October with kids is unacceptable.

comments.subject: landlord retaliation worry

comments.item_title: Citywide fourplex zoning reform
comments.subject: Opposed to upzoning single-family neighborhoods
comments.text:
Councilmember,

I OPPOSE allowing fourplexes on single-family lots citywide. I bought in a quiet part of the Rose Garden for the neighborhood character. Density belongs on transit corridors, not shoehorned onto every street with no parking plan.

I support affordable housing done right — this isn't it. Vote no.

[name removed]

comments.item_title: Citywide fourplex zoning reform
comments.subject: Please SUPPORT the fourplex reform
comments.text: I strongly SUPPORT legalizing fourplexes citywide. We have a housing shortage and single-family-only zoning is a big reason. More gentle density means teachers and nurses can live here. Please vote yes and ignore the fearmongering about 'character.'

comments.item_title: Citywide fourplex zoning reform
comments.subject: parking will be a nightmare
comments.text: My Almaden street already overflows with cars. Four units where one house was, times every lot, with no required parking? Oppose. At least require off-street parking.

comments.item_title: Citywide fourplex zoning reform
comments.subject: support but phase it
comments.text: I SUPPORT more housing but worry about doing it everywhere at once. Could the city phase it in near transit first and study the results? I lean yes but want it done thoughtfully.

comments.item_title: Citywide fourplex zoning reform
comments.subject: this is a giveaway to developers
comments.text: Let's be honest — 'fourplex reform' is a developer windfall dressed up as affordability. None of these will be affordable. I OPPOSE it. Require actual affordable units or forget it.

comments.item_title: Citywide fourplex zoning reform
comments.subject: A favor de más vivienda
comments.text:
Estimados concejales,

Apoyo permitir más unidades de vivienda en los vecindarios. Mis hijos adultos no pueden pagar renta aquí y tienen que irse de la ciudad. Necesitamos más opciones. Por favor voten a favor de la reforma. Gracias.

[name removed]

comments.item_title: Citywide fourplex zoning reform
comments.subject: historic districts exemption?
comments.text: Will historic neighborhoods be exempt? If not I strongly oppose. You'll destroy the fabric of places like Hanchett Park. Carve out protections or I'm a hard no.

comments.item_title: Citywide fourplex zoning reform
comments.subject: renters need you to say yes
comments.text: As a renter I SUPPORT this. The homeowners complaining already have theirs. More homes is how prices come down. Please vote yes for the rest of us.

comments.item_title: Citywide fourplex zoning reform
comments.subject: infrastructure can't handle it
comments.text: Sewers, water, schools — none of it is sized for 4x the people on every block. I OPPOSE upzoning until the city shows the infrastructure plan to support it. Put the cart behind the horse.

comments.item_title: Citywide fourplex zoning reform
comments.subject: mixed
comments.text: I see both sides. We need housing, but my block really can't take more cars. I honestly don't know which way I'd vote. Just want you to weigh neighborhood impacts seriously.

comments.item_title: Apartment Rent Ordinance amendment: annual rent-increase cap
comments.subject: Please support the rent stabilization amendment
comments.text:
Dear Councilmember,

I've rented the same one-bedroom near Japantown for seven years, and my rent rises every year. I strongly SUPPORT lowering the annual rent cap under the Apartment Rent Ordinance. Working people are being priced out of the city we grew up in. Please vote yes.
